cards.front: How is the human heart structured as a dual pump, and what are the specific roles of the right and left sides?
cards.back:
The heart consists of two separate but interconnected pumps operating in series:
  • Right Side: The right atrium receives deoxygenated systemic venous blood and delivers it into the right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary circulation to the lungs.
  • Left Side: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and delivers it into the left ventricle, which provides the primary high-pressure force to propel blood through the systemic/peripheral circulation to the rest of the body.

cards.front: What are the two major categories of heart valves, which specific valves belong to each, and what governs their opening and closing?
cards.back:
All heart valves open and close passively based on forward and backward pressure gradients:
  • Atrioventricular (AV) Valves: The tricuspid valve (right side) and mitral/bicuspid valve (left side); prevent retrograde backflow from ventricles into atria during ventricular contraction (systole).
  • Semilunar Valves: The aortic valve and pulmonary valve; prevent backflow from the aorta and pulmonary arteries into the ventricles during ventricular relaxation (diastole).

cards.front: Outline the sequential anatomical pathway of the cardiac electrical conduction system from impulse initiation to ventricular depolarization.
cards.back:
The electrical conduction impulse travels in the following sequence:
  1. Sinoatrial (SA) Node: The intrinsic pacemaker located in the right atrium that initiates rhythmic impulses.
  2. Internodal Pathways: Conduct the action potential across the atria to the AV node.
  3. Atrioventricular (AV) Node: Delays the electrical impulse slightly before allowing it to pass into the ventricles.
  4. Atrioventricular (AV) Bundle (Bundle of His): Conducts the impulse into the ventricles.
  5. Left & Right Bundle Branches & Purkinje Fibers: Rapidly disperse the impulse throughout the entire ventricular myocardium.

cards.front: Why is the slight electrical delay introduced at the atrioventricular (AV) node physiologically essential?
cards.back: The conductive delay at the AV node ensures that the electrical impulse does not travel into the ventricles too rapidly. This delay allows sufficient time for the atria to fully contract and empty their blood into the ventricles before ventricular contraction (systole) begins.

cards.front: Why does the sinoatrial (SA) node normally dominate and control heart rhythm over other potential cardiac pacemakers?
cards.back:
The SA node controls heart rhythm because its intrinsic discharge rate is considerably faster than downstream latent pacemakers:
  • SA Node: 60–80 discharges/min
  • AV Node: 40–60 discharges/min
  • Ventricular (Purkinje) Fibers: 15–40 discharges/min
Each SA node impulse sweeps through and depolarizes these excitable tissues before they can reach self-excitation threshold spontaneously.

cards.front: How do sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves modulate resting and exercise heart rates, and what are the clinical heart rate thresholds?
cards.back:
The cardiovascular center of the medulla transmits autonomic impulses to the heart:
  • Sympathetic Stimulation: Accelerates SA node depolarization (the chronotropic effect) and increases heart rate and myocardial contractility.
  • Parasympathetic Stimulation: Slower SA node discharge rate via acetylcholine release, reducing heart rate.
Clinical Thresholds: Normal resting heart rate is 60 to 100 beats/min; fewer than 60 beats/min is bradycardia, while greater than 100 beats/min is tachycardia.

cards.front: What physiological cardiac events correspond to the P-wave, QRS complex, and T-wave on a standard surface electrocardiogram (ECG)?
cards.back:
• P-Wave: Electrical depolarization of the atria, which directly initiates atrial mechanical contraction.
  • QRS Complex: Electrical depolarization of the ventricles, triggering ventricular contraction (systole). Note: Atrial repolarization occurs simultaneously but is masked on the ECG by the large QRS complex.
  • T-Wave: Electrical repolarization of the ventricles as they recover during diastole.

cards.front: Contrast the structural characteristics and primary physiological functions of arteries, arterioles, capillaries, and veins.
cards.back:
• Arteries: Rapidly transport blood pumped from the heart under high pressure; possess strong, elastic muscular walls.
  • Arterioles: Small muscular branches that act as control valves; constrict or dilate extensively to regulate blood flow entering capillaries based on tissue metabolic demand.
  • Capillaries: Thin, permeable microvessels with single-endothelial walls allowing bidirectional exchange of oxygen, fluid, nutrients, electrolytes, and hormones with interstitial fluid.
  • Veins & Venules: Collect blood from capillaries and transport it under low pressure back to the heart; compliant walls allow veins to act as a dynamic blood reservoir, and leg veins feature one-way valves to prevent retrograde pooling.

cards.front: What two vital physiological functions does hemoglobin perform in blood during exercise?
cards.back:
Hemoglobin, an iron–protein molecule carried by red blood cells, serves two primary roles:
  • Oxygen Transport: Binds oxygen in pulmonary capillaries and transports it to exercising tissues for cellular aerobic metabolism.
  • Acid–Base Buffer: Acts as a crucial regulator of hydrogen ion (H⁺) concentration, buffering exercise-induced cellular acidosis to preserve chemical reaction rates.

cards.front: How do red blood cells facilitate the removal of carbon dioxide (CO2), the most abundant metabolic by-product, from exercising tissues?
cards.back: Red blood cells contain large quantities of the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the reversible chemical reaction between carbon dioxide and water (\(\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{HCO}_3^-\)), allowing \(\text{CO}_2\) to be transported primarily as soluble bicarbonate in the blood back to the lungs for expiration.
